seismicShadow.title: Reading an interior from what never arrives
seismicShadow.subtitle: Sweep a seismometer around the planet and watch the shear wave disappear
seismicShadow.aria: A cross-section of a planet with seismic ray paths from a source at the top to a station at a variable angle; past 103 degrees the shear wave arrival is absent
seismicShadow.hint: Shear waves need rigidity. A liquid has none, so a shear wave simply cannot cross a molten outer core — and past about 103° of arc, every path to the station must go through it. The station falls silent. That silence, mapped all the way around the planet in 1914, is how we learned the core was liquid without ever going there. Set the core solid and the silence vanishes.
seismicShadow.distanceLabel: Angle from the quake to the station

arrival.precursor: Faint, via the solid inner core

verdict.shadowRange: Shear shadow runs from {from}° to the far side; compression returns at {to}°
verdict.noShadow: No shadow anywhere — every station hears both waves

mantleRayleigh.title: Does the layer overturn, or just conduct?
mantleRayleigh.subtitle: One dimensionless number decides whether a mantle stirs itself
mantleRayleigh.aria: A logarithmic bar showing the Rayleigh number against its critical threshold, with markers for Earth, Pandora and the Moon
mantleRayleigh.hint: Buoyancy fights viscosity, and the Rayleigh number is the scorecard. Below a threshold of a few hundred, hot rock at the bottom simply loses the argument and heat trickles upward by conduction. Above it, the layer overturns. Notice how little the temperature slider moves the answer compared to the viscosity slider — that exponent is why a mantle a few hundred degrees hotter behaves like a different substance.
mantleRayleigh.nuNote: Times what conduction alone would deliver

verdict.convectsNote: Rock circulates; heat rides the flow to the surface
verdict.conductsNote: Rock stays put; heat seeps through it slowly

tectonicRegime.title: Which kind of crust does a world end up with?
tectonicRegime.subtitle: Heat flowing out, against the strength of the lid it has to escape through
tectonicRegime.aria: A two-axis map of surface heat flux against lithospheric yield strength, shaded by tectonic regime, with markers for Earth, Venus, Mars and Io and a dashed box covering Pandora's plausible range
tectonicRegime.hint: No planet decides whether to have tectonics. Its mantle convects regardless; the only question is whether the stress arriving underneath the crust can break it. Two numbers settle that, and Earth sits in a narrow corner of the map where the answer is barely yes. Pandora is drawn as a box rather than a dot because canon fixes its heat but says nothing at all about how strong or how wet its crust is — and the box crosses every boundary.
tectonicRegime.axisFlux: Heat leaving the surface (W/m², log scale)

regimeNote.mobileLid: The lid breaks, sinks, and is remade — Earth's arrangement
regimeNote.sluggishLid: The lid deforms slowly without breaking into plates
regimeNote.stagnantLid: A single unbroken shell; heat conducts through it — Venus, Mars
regimeNote.heatPipe: Melt carries the heat out and buries the old surface — Io

burialMountain.title: Two ways to raise a mountain

subtitle.burial: Bury a crust deep enough and the sphere itself squeezes it upward
subtitle.collision: Thickened light crust floating on heavier rock

aria.burial: A cross-section of crust buried under stacked lava sheets, compressed inward, with a fault-bounded block thrust upward along a deep thrust fault
aria.collision: A cross-section of two converging plates raising a folded mountain range with a deep buoyant crustal root beneath it

hint.burial: Io has mountains eighteen kilometres tall and not one plate boundary. Lava buries its surface at roughly a centimetre a year, and buried crust sinks — but a shrinking sphere has less room at depth than at the top, so the crust is forced into enormous sideways compression. Eventually it fails, and slabs of it are shoved into the sky. Tall peaks are not proof of colliding continents.
hint.collision: Earth's ranges float. Continental crust is lighter than the mantle beneath it, so a thickened pile sits high the way an iceberg does — and hides most of itself below. That hidden root is the giveaway: measure a mountain's gravity and you learn whether it is buoyant, or merely propped up.

oreGenesis.title: Where ore comes from — and what it needs
oreGenesis.subtitle: Five routes from ordinary rock to a deposit worth mining
oreGenesis.aria: A bar chart of five ore-forming pathways by enrichment factor, with the ones unavailable in the selected tectonic regime dimmed and marked closed
oreGenesis.hint: A metal at a few parts per million is worthless; at a thousand times that it is a mine. Every route to that concentration has requirements, and most of the rich ones on Earth need a plate boundary, circulating water, or both — which is why terrestrial ore sits in predictable belts rather than scattered at random. Switch the regime and watch which routes close. A world with no moving crust can still make ore. It has a much harder time making the richest kind.

pathway.arcHydrothermal: Hot fluids above a sinking slab
pathway.sedimentary: Sorted by water at the surface

requirement.magmatic: Needs only a magma body cooling slowly — available to any volcanic world
requirement.arcHydrothermal: Needs water carried down a sinking slab and released into rising magma
requirement.ridgeVms: Needs seawater circulating through hot young crust at a spreading axis
requirement.orogenicGold: Needs a collisional belt cooking water out of buried rock
requirement.sedimentary: Needs rivers, rain and a surface that keeps being renewed
